rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate all six peaks while limiting the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The retention window and critical-pair resolutions will guide subsequent gradient and temperature adjustments.
Injection 1 already achieved the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient by one step to seek a faster fully resolved method, retaining injection 1 as the benchmark.

The 8-minute gradient retains ample resolution, with minimum R of 3.47 and maximum CRF. Shorten by another grid step while holding composition and temperature fixed to test a faster fully resolved method.
Shorten the gradient one more step to reduce elution time while testing whether the closest pair remains above R = 1.5. The 6-minute method remains a fully resolved fallback with maximum CRF.

Test the minimum gradient duration to establish the speed–resolution boundary; the closest pair may fall below R = 1.5. If it does, retain the fully resolved 4-minute gradient as the benchmark for temperature and composition refinement.
Back off to the fully resolved 4-minute gradient and raise temperature one step to test faster elution and temperature selectivity. Monitor the early critical pair, whose resolution was 1.83 at 40 C.

Higher temperature compressed the critical early pair, so test lower temperature with a slightly shallower 2-minute gradient to recover its resolution. The 0.80 final organic fraction should still elute the last compound promptly during the hold.

Raise final organic by one step to accelerate the last peak while retaining the favorable low-temperature selectivity. This tests whether the early pair's R = 1.59 margin can tolerate a slightly steeper gradient.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to reduce gradient slope while keeping the stronger final wash. Test whether this restores the marginal early pair to R ≥ 1.5 while preserving faster last-peak elution than injection 7.

Shift both gradient endpoints upward one step, preserving the slope that gave full resolution in injection 9. The stronger endpoint should accelerate the last peak; monitor the early pair for loss of retention or selectivity.

Shift the gradient window upward another step while preserving its slope and low-temperature selectivity. This should shorten last-peak retention further, provided the early pair remains sufficiently retained and resolved.

Raise only the starting organic fraction to narrow the gradient window and seek faster elution at the maximum endpoint strength. Check whether the shallower slope preserves early-pair resolution despite reduced initial retention.
Use the improved early-pair resolution margin to test a one-step temperature increase for faster last-peak elution. Keep the gradient fixed to measure temperature selectivity in this narrower window.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to test further time reduction while retaining the maximum CRF. The first peak is now near the gradient-arrival time, so this run will establish whether reduced initial retention compromises the early pair.

Back off the starting organic fraction to restore early retention, then test the next temperature step to establish the speed–resolution boundary. Injection 13 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method if this increase pushes the critical pair below R = 1.5.

Return to 30 C and lower the endpoint one step to seek more resolution margin with only a small retention-time cost. Injection 13 remains the fastest fully resolved benchmark; this run tests a potentially more robust maximum-CRF alternative.

Test whether cooling restores early-pair resolution at the higher starting organic fraction that failed at 30 C. This checks the remaining nearby composition boundary while retaining injection 13 as the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method.

Shift both endpoints down one step from injection 13, preserving slope while moving the early peaks away from the dead-time region. This tests a less initial-retention-sensitive alternative that may retain maximum CRF with only a modest time cost.

Cool injection 16 by one step to increase the critical-pair resolution margin while keeping a short 2-minute gradient. The maximum CRF is already secured; this tests a more tolerant alternative to the fastest fully resolved method, injection 13.

Lower the starting organic fraction from injection 19 to move the early peaks farther from the dead time, while retaining low-temperature selectivity. This tests a nearby maximum-CRF alternative with better initial retention; injection 13 remains the fastest fully resolved benchmark.

Narrow the gradient window from injection 18 to improve its marginal early-pair resolution while keeping the early peaks away from the dead time. This tests a nearby fully resolved alternative; injection 13 remains the fastest demonstrated method with maximum CRF.

Test the remaining close neighbor of the fastest fully resolved method, injection 13, using lower starting organic to improve initial retention. This checks whether the maximum endpoint strength still permits full resolution at 30 C without the longer hold-phase elution of injection 21.

Cool injection 21 one step to seek greater critical-pair resolution while retaining a short gradient and adequate initial retention. Injection 13 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method; this tests a nearby alternative with more resolution margin.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step from injection 23 to test a slightly faster alternative with comparable resolution margin. Keep injection 13 as the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method, since the maximum CRF has already been reached.

Raise temperature one step from injection 24 to shorten elution while testing whether its resolution margin preserves maximum CRF. Injection 13 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method at t_last = 2.58 min.
